tools.what_it_times: It depends on the command. With both -writers and -readers in one SBK process (Action Write_Reading) it measures end to end: each writer stamps time.getCurrentTime() into the first 8 bytes of the payload and records nothing itself, and each reader subtracts that stamp from its own time.getCurrentTime() (PerL computes endTime - startTime). With writers only it times the write call to completion; with readers only, the read call. In SBK's own end-to-end mode both readings are in one JVM. But the stamp travels inside the record, and the reader subtracts whoever wrote it. SBK-GEM runs the same arguments, mixed writer-plus-reader workloads included, on several hosts against one target, and the Kafka driver puts every reader in one consumer group named after the topic. So a record stamped on one host can be subtracted on another. The Kafka reader applies the first record's stamp in each poll to every record in that poll. Whether a driver supports end to end at all is per driver

clock_and_resolution.finding: Chosen with -time; the default is timeUnit=ms. ms means System.currentTimeMillis(): the wall clock in whole milliseconds, possibly coarser per the JDK. mcs means System.nanoTime()/1000; ns means System.nanoTime(). The JDK 25 javadoc (SBK builds with Java 25) says nanoTime counts from an arbitrary per-JVM origin, possibly negative, and has meaning only as a difference within one JVM. An mcs or ns stamp subtracted in another JVM is therefore meaningless, and an ms stamp across hosts carries their clock offset. SBM rejects a client whose time unit differs from its own, but nothing ties mcs or ns to a single JVM

tools.what_it_times: Two latencies, kept apart by client side. The subscriber side is end to end: the publisher writes its wall-clock milliseconds into a 'sendTime' message attribute, and on receipt the subscriber subtracts that from its own wall-clock milliseconds. The publisher side is publish latency, from publish start to success of the publish future, in the same process. Java, Go, Python and Node clients each implement this, and the publisher and subscriber of a run use the same language. In the default GCE mode (--local and --in_process both default to false) each client type gets its own managed instance group, so the two end-to-end stamps come from different machines. After the burn-in period the Java controller adds up the clients' log-1.5 histograms, logs the 50, 99 and 99.9 percentiles, and writes the bucket midpoints for 50, 90, 99 and 99.9 to output.csv.

clock_and_resolution.finding: Every language uses a wall clock at millisecond resolution: Java System.currentTimeMillis(); Go time.Now().UnixNano() divided by one million (UnixNano tells time, so it reads the wall clock, not the monotonic reading); Python int(time.time()*1000); Node (new Date).getTime(). The end-to-end value subtracts the publisher VM's wall clock from the subscriber VM's. Nothing in the code synchronises, measures or corrects the offset between them. Values are whole milliseconds, binned by floor(log base 1.5), so results are reported as bucket bounds or midpoints, not as measured values. clock_and_resolution.finding: Every arrow stamps whole milliseconds from a wall clock. The default C arrow uses clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) truncated to ms. C++ uses system_clock in ms, Python int(time.time()*1000), JavaScript Date().getTime().
